catalog_quote: A heavy syllable in Ditidaht is one that contains a long vowel (coda consonants do not affect syllable weight). Second, after the initial foot, syllables are unfooted unless they can be incorporated into LH́ or H́ feet. The data in (33) exemplify Ditidaht's entirely regular stress pattern. ... Stress placement obeys the following generalizations. First, syllables with long vowels are always stressed. Second, syllables with short vowels are stressed only in monosyllables (33a), and in second syllables following an initial syllable that also contains a short vowel (33b). Third, the first stress is the primary (strongest) one. I conclude, first, that only long vowels contribute to syllable weight, since only syllables containing long vowels attract stress, regardless of their position in the word. ... (34) a. Feet are iambic, built left-to-right, main stress left. b. Long vowels contribute…
sweep_summary: Ditidaht has a single stress-titled bibliography item, Werle 2007 (CJL 52), which is already the catalog's deciding source and is held by the project in full (author PDF via the Internet Archive; Crossref DOI 10.1017/S0008413100004205 added). Re-read: sec. 4.1 pp. 91-92 confirms the catalog's weight-sensitive coding verbatim (long vowel = heavy, codas weightless, primary stress on syllable 1 if heavy else syllable 2, later long vowels secondary, 'entirely regular'). Werle 2010 (Wakashan phonology ms., sec. 4.2) independently confirms the peninitial all-light default (#LĹ hawłíy vs #H́L dúusaq). Beyond the item list, this search of works with stress in the title downloaded the two classic open descriptions from Werle's kwistuup.net mirror (Thomas & Hess 1981, 250 pp; Swadesh & Swadesh 1933, IJAL 7) and Klokeid 1975 (ERIC): none says anything about stress or accent (Swadesh & Swadesh describe only variable vowel length in the second syllable; Thomas & Hess's orthography marks length, not stress), and Werle 2002 states that before his work stress had been described only for Makah and Tseshaht Nuu-chah-nulth. No source contradicts or refines the catalog; nothing remains to acquire.org, Glottolog, Werle's UVic page and kwistuup.net; the pre-existing held by the project is a generic 200-row page with no Wakashan entries, not a Ditidaht reference list.

new_statements.reading: Primary stress sits in the first two syllables and is decided by vowel length: initial syllable if it has a long vowel, otherwise the second syllable (also when both are short: ba.búʔ, ka.lá); monosyllables are stressed. Every later long-vowel syllable gets secondary stress; later short-vowel syllables stay unstressed. Weight = long vowel only, codas weightless. This is exactly the catalog's 'weight' coding (weight-sensitive with a fixed default, CVV heavy, left-edge two-syllable window, all-light default peninitial); Werle 2010 sec. 4.2 restates it comparatively (hawłíy vs dúusaq).

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation, the domain quotation and the footnote are all verbatim at the stated pages (pp. 91-92 ex. 33-34; pp. 79-80; fn. 6 p. 78) in the held author's PDF of Werle 2007. (2) The classification (weight-sensitive, CVV heavy, codas weightless, left-edge two-syllable window, iambic L-to-R with main stress leftmost, secondary stress on later long vowels) is exactly Werle's generalizations and analysis (34a-d), and Werle 2010 sec. 4.2 (held) restates it with fresh examples. (3) Against Glottolog's list, Werle 2007 is the sole phonology work; the alternatives are a 1981 introductory textbook, a Japanese encyclopaedia sketch and syntax papers; Werle 2002 (downloaded now, open) confirms no Ditidaht stress description existed before 2007. No instrumental or dissertation-level study of Ditidaht prosody was found. (4) Hence well-sourced; works still to obtain are low-priority c

sources.note: Primary stress is confined to the first two syllables and is weight-driven: the initial syllable if it has a long vowel (#H́L, #H́H), otherwise the second syllable (#LH́, #LĹ); monosyllables stressed; every later long-vowel syllable takes secondary stress, later short-vowel syllables are unstressed/unfooted. Weight = long vowel only; coda consonants weightless (fn. 6: 'consonants never bear stress, nor even contribute to syllable weight'). sources.quote: In the southern languages, primary stress is on the first or second syllable of the word. Long vowels contribute to syllable weight, but coda nasals in Nuu-chah-ulth are the only consonants that do so ... All southern languages stress the first syllable if it is heavy (#H́L, #H́H), and the second if it is heavier than the first (#LH́). But Nuu-chah-nulth gives two initial light syllables trochaic stress (#ĹL), while Ditidaht and Makah prefer iambic stress (#LĹ): ... D #LĹ hawłíy 'ready' #H́L dúusaq 'sort of, so-so'
sources.note: Comparative restatement by the same author: Ditidaht primary stress on syllable 1 if heavy, else syllable 2; all-light default is peninitial (iambic #LĹ, hawłíy), unlike Nuu-chah-nulth (#ĹL). Reports variant patterns only for Makah and Ahousaht Nuu-chah-nulth, none for Ditidaht.

sources.quote: 'In the dialects for which stress is described - Makah and Tseshaht Nuuchahnulth - stress is restricted to the first two syllables. I argue that Makah builds an iambic foot over the first one or two syllables.' Ditidaht is cited only for final short-vowel deletion and syncope (Swadesh & Swadesh 1933), not for stress.
sources.locator: sec. 1 (intro), p. 1-2 of paper; sec. 2.1 'Stress' (Makah); Tseshaht stress discussion
sources.note: States that as of 2002 stress had been described only for Makah and Tseshaht Nuu-chah-nulth, not Ditidaht; Ditidaht is discussed only for final-vowel deletion and syncope (Swadesh & Swadesh 1933; Jacobsen 1979a). No Ditidaht stress statement.

sources.quote: The length of certain suffix vowels is variable. Such vowels are long when occurring in the second syllable of the word; otherwise, they are short and subject to syncope (see rules of sandhi given below).
sources.note: No mention of stress or accent (a full-text search for stress/accent: zero hits); the sketch treats variable vowel length keyed to the second syllable and syncope, i.e. the prosodic phenomena Werle 2007 later relates to footing, but says nothing about stress placement.
